meta.title: Who really said "The first thing is character, before money or anything else. Money cannot buy it. A man I do not trust could not get money from me on all the bonds in Christendom"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: J. P. Morgan really said it — under oath to the Pujo Committee, 19 December 1912. The popular one-sentence version splices three separate answers.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The first thing is character, before money or anything else. Money cannot buy it. A man I do not trust could not get money from me on all the bonds in Christendom'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes — verbatim from his Pujo Committee testimony, 19 December 1912, page 1084 of the printed hearings. The one-line form is a compression.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Morgan said it under oath on Thursday, 19 December 1912, answering the committee’s counsel Samuel Untermyer, and the words are printed verbatim on page 1084 of Part 15 of the House Money Trust Investigation hearings. The familiar single sentence is a compression: in the transcript these are three separate answers, and the last one begins “Because…”

source.heading: The congressional record, page 1084

docMeta.dd: Samuel Untermyer, counsel to the Pujo subcommittee

source.excerpt:
Mr. Untermyer. Is not commercial credit based primarily upon money or property?
Mr. Morgan. No, sir; the first thing is character.
Mr. Untermyer. Before money or property?
Mr. Morgan. Before money or anything else. Money can not buy it.
…
Mr. Untermyer. He does not get it on his face or his character, does he?
Mr. Morgan. Yes; he gets it on his character.
Mr. Untermyer. I see; then he might as well take the bonds home, had he not?
Mr. Morgan. Because a man I do not trust could not get money from me on all the bonds in Christendom.
trail: Wikiquote files the line in its sourced section, under “Testimony to the Pujo Committee (1912),” and prints it with the seams showing — ellipses and a bracketed [in credit]: J. P. Morgan on Wikiquote ↗.

The transcript itself survives in full. The Government Printing Office issued Morgan’s second day on the stand as Part 15 of the Money Trust Investigation hearings, headed “Washington, D. C., Thursday, December 19, 1912”; the character exchange runs down page 1084 — full plain text at the Internet Archive ↗.

A Harvard Joint Center for History and Economics working paper opens with the same exchange and footnotes it to “Part 15, December 19, 1912. p. 1084” — Kelly J. Peeler, The Rise and Fall of J. Pierpont Morgan (2010) ↗.

author.name: J. P. Morgan
author.heading: Who was J. P. Morgan?
author.bio: John Pierpont Morgan dominated American corporate finance for a generation, assembling railroads, U.S. Steel and General Electric out of warring firms and twice acting as a private lender of last resort to the United States Treasury. By December 1912 he was seventy-five, and the House subcommittee investigating the “money trust” had put him on the stand to explain how so few houses came to sit astride the nation’s credit. He died in Rome on 31 March 1913, roughly three months later; this testimony was his last great public performance.

misattribution.heading: Genuine — but not as it usually travels
misattribution.intro: Nothing here is invented. The words are Morgan’s, on the congressional record, under oath. What travels badly is the packaging — and the company the line keeps.

items.why: Wikiquote prints it with the joins visible: “The first thing [in credit] is character … before money or anything else. Money cannot buy it.… A man I do not trust could not get money from me on all the bonds in Christendom.” Delete the ellipses and the bracket and you get the version that circulates — smooth, quotable, and no longer a transcript. Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗

items.who: “Gold is money. Everything else is credit.”
items.why: This is the line most often pinned to the same 1912 testimony, and quote sites run it as Morgan with no source and no date — AZQuotes, for one ↗. What the transcript records, a few pages earlier on p. 1081, is blunter and less symmetrical: “That is an evidence of banking, but it is not the money itself. Money is gold, and nothing else.” The polished inversion appears in neither day’s printed transcript — read Part 15 and check ↗

items.who: “If you have to ask the price, you can’t afford it.”
items.why: The yacht line is the other Morgan quotation everyone knows, and Wikiquote keeps it in its Attributed section, tracing it no further back than a 1961 trade magazine, Business Education World. The character line is a different order of evidence: it is in the congressional record. Compare the two sections ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Every word of the popular sentence is Morgan’s own, spoken to Samuel Untermyer on 19 December 1912 and printed on page 1084 of Part 15 of the Money Trust Investigation hearings ↗. Only the seams are modern.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The Pujo subcommittee sat from May 1912 to January 1913 with one question in front of it: had a handful of Wall Street houses quietly taken hold of the country’s credit? Counsel Samuel Untermyer had Morgan on the stand for two days, 18 and 19 December 1912, and on the second morning he tried to close a simple trap — credit rests on money and property, so whoever controls the money controls the credit. Morgan, then seventy-five, refused the premise outright.

It is a strange answer from a man being investigated as a monopolist, and that is exactly why it stuck: the most powerful lender in America, at the peak of an anti-monopoly inquiry, insisting that the thing he actually lends against is trust. He died in Rome on 31 March 1913, roughly three months after saying it. The subcommittee wound up that January, and its findings fed the Federal Reserve Act, the Clayton Anti-trust Act and the Federal Trade Commission — the machinery built so that no single banker’s character would ever matter that much again.
context.detailsSummary: What Untermyer was actually driving at
detailsBody: Untermyer’s next questions on page 1084 are the giveaway. If character is really the basis of credit, he asks, why do banks demand a statement of what a man owns before they lend? Morgan’s reply: “That is what they go into; but the first thing they say is, ‘We want to see your record.’” Pressed on a borrower who puts up government or railroad bonds, Morgan still insists the credit rides on the man — which is where the Christendom line lands, as a retort rather than an aphorism.

The pull quote above comes from the same page, and is the reason the exchange reads as boast rather than piety: Morgan volunteered that he had handed a man a million-dollar check knowing he had not a cent. Untermyer’s dry follow-up — “That is not business?” — got the answer “Yes; unfortunately it is. I do not think it is good business, though.”
context.pull: I have known a man to come into my office, and I have given him a check for a million dollars when I knew he had not a cent in the world.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists the line in its sourced section under "Testimony to the Pujo Committee (1912)", rendered with ellipses and a bracketed [in credit], cited to Morgan's testimony before the House Bank and Currency Committee, December 18-19, 1912; its separate "Attributed" section holds "If you have to ask the price, you can't afford it", cited to Business Education World (1961). The page gives Morgan's dates as April 17, 1837 - March 31, 1913.

The Internet Archive holds Part 15 (volume 15) of "Money trust investigation: investigation of financial and monetary conditions in the United States under House resolutions nos. 429 and 504, before a subcommittee of the Committee on Banking and Currency", Government Printing Office, 1913, with full text readable and downloadable.

The full OCR text of Part 15 is headed "Washington, D. C., Thursday, December 19, 1912" and "TESTIMONY OF MR. J. PIERPONT MORGAN - Continued", and contains on page 1084 the verbatim exchange: "Mr. Untermyer. Is not commercial credit based primarily upon money or property? / Mr. Morgan. No, sir; the first thing is character. / Mr. Untermyer. Before money or property? / Mr. Morgan. Before money or anything else. Money can not buy it." and, further down the same page, "Mr. Morgan. Because a man I do not trust could not get money from me on all the bonds in Christendom." It also contains on page 1081 "That is an evidence of banking, but it is not the money itself. Money is gold, and nothing else." and on page 1084 "I have known a man to come into my office, and I have given him a check for a million dollars when I knew he had not a cent in the world." plus "That is what they go into; but the first thing they say is, 'We want to see your record.'" The phrases "gold is money" and "everything else is credit" do not appear in this volume.

Kelly J. Peeler's Harvard Joint Center for History and Economics working paper "The Rise and Fall of J. Pierpont Morgan" (April 2010) opens with the Untermyer-Morgan character exchange, dates it 19 December 1912 in Washington D.C., and footnotes it as "Money Trust Investigation ... Part 15, December 19, 1912. p. 1084." Its footnotes give Untermyer's dates as March 6, 1858 - March 16, 1940, Morgan's as April 17, 1837 - March 31, 1913, and the Pujo Committee's span as May 1912 to January 1913.

J. P. Morgan was born 17 April 1837 in Hartford, Connecticut and died 31 March 1913 in Rome, Italy, aged 75; he was an American financier and investment banker who dominated corporate finance on Wall Street; he testified before the Pujo Committee in December 1912 and died roughly three months later.

The Pujo Committee was a US congressional subcommittee of the House Committee on Banking and Currency, active 1912-1913, chaired by Arsene Pujo of Louisiana with Samuel Untermyer as counsel, investigating the "money trust"; its work led to the Clayton Anti-trust Act, the Federal Trade Commission and the Federal Reserve.

Samuel Untermyer (March 6, 1858 - March 16, 1940) was counsel-investigator to the Pujo Committee and famously cross-examined J. P. Morgan and other New York bankers. The article does not itself quote the character-and-credit exchange.
AZQuotes presents "Gold is money. Everything else is credit." attributed to J. P. Morgan, with no source document and no date given.
